title: The Goblin's Missing Ribbons
markdown:
Perched high on the pine-dark slopes of Owlglass Mountain lived Eira, a young elf whose eyes sparkled like dew-kissed spiderwebs. Her dearest friend was Lumina, a witch with a heart as warm as a hearth fire. Lumina’s cottage among whispering ferns smelled of lavender and starlight simmering in a pot. Eira’s home was a hollowed oak, cozy with pine.

One crisp evening, apricot and rose on the peaks, Eira found Lumina by her toadstool garden. The little fungi glowed with their own soft light.

“Lumina. Have you noticed something strange? Something quite peculiar?”

Lumina tended a grumpy puffball, spectacles on her nose. “What has caught your elf-sight? Is it the way the moon is getting ready to wink?”

“The ribbons.” A delicate finger toward the well-worn path, where cheerful streamers used to wave like little flags. “They’re gone. Not one or two. Many. The path feels naked.”

Lumina’s eyes narrowed, not with worry, with curiosity. “Missing ribbons. After dusk. A curious happening.”

“As if borrowed by the wind, or a mischievous sprite.”

“Then it’s time for a little adventure. Warmest cloak. We shall follow the trail before the moon is high.”

And so, as the first stars pricked through the twilight like tiny diamond pins, the elf and the witch set off. The forest floor was soft with fallen pine needles, muffling their footsteps. The air grew cool and crisp, carrying damp earth and distant fir. They followed the winding path, looking for any stray thread, any clue. Off the main trail, where shadows grew deep: mushrooms stacked in wobbly towers that seemed to defy gravity, tied with the missing lantern ribbons, fluttering quite out of place.

Then a faint reedy sound, a mournful sigh on a blade of grass, also oddly cheerful and bouncy. They crept, quiet as shadows on moss, pushed aside a curtain of damp fragrant ferns.

In a clearing lit by glow-worms sat a little green-skinned goblin, enormous floppy ears nearly to his shoulders, wide earnest eyes on a peculiar instrument: a large puffball mushroom, colourful ribbons tied so they danced when he played. He puffed air through hollow reeds in the cap. A happy wiggle of a tune. A jig for toes.

“He’s decorating his instruments,” Lumina whispered. “How very creative.”

The goblin—Pipkin, they would learn—stopped. Ears shot up. He clutched the mushroom. “Hello?” Rustling leaves.

Eira stepped forward, smile a sunbeam. “Hello, little one. We’re Eira and Lumina. We’ve come about the ribbons. They’re very pretty, aren’t they?”

Ears drooped like wilted petals. “You don’t like my music?” A small tear.

“Your music is very interesting. It makes you want to wiggle your toes. Like a sunny day after rain. But those ribbons belong to the travellers who walk these paths at night. They help them see, so they don’t trip over roots or get lost.”

Lumina’s smile crinkled her eyes. “Little friendly guides, showing the way home.”

Pipkin looked at the ribbons, then at them. “I thought they were just pretty things to make my mushroom-flutes extra festive. I didn’t know they were for guiding people. I just love making my music sound happy. I’m sorry. I’ve never thought about travellers needing guides.”

Scattered, not unkind. Floppy ears drooped with true regret.

“Accidents happen when you’re busy making wonderful music,” Lumina said, kneeling. “We have lovely soft moss, and these bright red berries are quite cheerful. They’ll flutter just as nicely, and they won’t lead anyone astray.”

They gathered velvety moss and shiny berries, tied them to the instruments. Pipkin played a new tune, tinkling bells and happy hops, moss bobbing, berries gleaming. He promised, with a solemn nod that made his ears sway, to ask before borrowing, and to ask travellers if they’d like to hear his music.

Walking home, moon making dewdrops into tiny diamonds, they retied the last few ribbons on the path branches so travellers would have their friendly guides again. Eira felt a warm glow, far warmer than her cloak. Pipkin’s jig followed them a little way, then stayed in the clearing, where it belonged, moss bobbing, berries gleaming, no lanterns led astray.

And so Eira and Lumina learned that pretty things may already have a job, and a goblin who asks first can keep both his tune and his neighbours’ way home.
